screens.title: What is Tracing (Raycasting)?
screens.narratorSegment: Tracing is the act of casting an invisible probe — a line or swept shape — through the game world to detect what it intersects. Think of a flashlight beam that reports the first object it hits. In Unreal Engine, traces are performed using C++ APIs that accept start and end points, or start/end with a shape size, and return an FHitResult containing who was hit and where. The practical value is broad: you use a line trace to detect what the player is looking at for interactions, and shape traces to test volumes such as a melee swing or explosion sweep. An important detail is that traces do not move actors; they only ask the physics and collision system which objects intersect the probe. This keeps traces cheap conceptually, but cost accumulates when you run many complex traces each frame. As a quick concrete example, if you want a player to pick up a key they see on a table, cast a line from the camera forward a short distance, check the hit, verify the actor implements your interaction interface, and then execute the pickup. A common misconception is to assume a trace always returns usable pointers; always check the hit flag before accessing actor, component, or hit location. The core takeaway is that tracing gives you precise information about line of sight and overlaps when set up with appropriate collision and query parameters.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A trace casts a ray or shape into the world and reports collisions; it’s a query, not a physics force.

content.html:
Core Concept Tracing (Raycasting)

Tracing explained

A query that asks: what does this ray or swept shape intersect in the world?

Intuition & analogy

Imagine a flashlight beam. A line trace finds the first object lit by the beam. A sphere sweep is like pushing a ball through space and seeing what it touches.

When to use
  • Line trace for precise look or hitscan interactions.
  • Shape trace for area attacks and volume checks.
  • Debug traces to verify collision setup during development.
Common misconception
Assuming a hit is always valid. You must check the hit flag before using hit data to avoid null dereferences.
Key Takeaway

Tracing queries the world for collisions; use the right shape and check results before using them.

Concrete example
Highlighting an object: cast a short line trace from the player camera, ignore the player, check for a blocking hit, and toggle the render custom depth on the hit component to show a highlight.
Explanation points
  • Start and end define the path; shape traces need an extent or radius.
  • Collision channels determine which objects respond to the trace.
  • FCollisionQueryParams allow ignoring actors and toggling complex tracing.
Analogy card
Flashlight: a thin ray; rolling a ball: a swept shape checking volume intersections.
Why it matters
Reliable detection underpins pickup, targeting, and AI sensing systems.

screens.title: Performing a Line Trace in C++
screens.narratorSegment: Performing a line trace in C++ follows a clear sequence: pick a start point, compute an end point, configure your query parameters, call the trace A P I, visualize for debugging, and then interpret the FHitResult. Start by choosing the correct origin — typically the player camera or pawn view location — and compute the end point by adding the forward vector scaled by your trace distance. Next, set up an FCollisionQueryParams object to ignore the tracing actor and configure whether you want complex collision. Call LineTraceSingleByChannel on the world, supplying the collision channel such as visibility or a custom channel. The function returns a boolean indicating whether a blocking hit occurred and fills an FHitResult with fields like actor, component, location, and normal. Always test the returned boolean or bBlockingHit before using any pointers. Use debug helpers to draw a line in green for hits or red for misses; this visual feedback makes logic errors obvious. For multiple objects along the path use multi-trace variants. A frequent mistake is performing traces every frame unnecessarily; prefer running them on input or at a reduced frequency when possible. By following these steps you get a predictable, debuggable trace that converts into concrete gameplay responses, like picking up, highlighting, or shooting an object.

keyIdea.title: Trace steps
keyIdea.text: Start + direction -> query params -> call trace -> check hit -> use hit data safely; visualize during development.

content.html:
Process Flow Line Trace Steps

Line trace: step-by-step

  1. Choose origin: get pawn view or camera location and rotation.
  2. Compute end: add forward vector times desired range.
  3. Set QueryParams: ignore self, choose bTraceComplex as needed.
  4. Call trace: use LineTraceSingleByChannel or Multi variant.
  5. Check result: verify the boolean or bBlockingHit and then read actor/location safely.
Key Takeaway

Follow a deterministic sequence and use debug drawing to validate behaviour early.

Supporting details
  • Choose an appropriate trace distance; too short and you miss intended targets, too long and you waste checks.
  • Query params can also return physical material information if needed for material-based effects.
  • Use ECC_Visibility for view-based interactions or a custom GameTraceChannel for gameplay-specific filtering.
Concrete example
From camera location, trace 500 units forward, ignore the character, use visibility channel, draw a green line on hit, and call an interaction interface on the hit actor.
Common mistake
Not ignoring the tracing actor causes self-hits. Also, assuming non-blocking hits contain valid actor pointers is unsafe.

screens.title: C++ Example: Interaction Trace and Highlighting
screens.narratorSegment: Now we walk through a practical C++ implementation that highlights an actor the player is looking at. The essential flow is: compute start and end, set up FHitResult and FCollisionQueryParams, call LineTraceSingleByChannel, and conditionally toggle the render custom depth on the hit actor’s root component. The example uses GetPawnViewLocation and the pawn view rotation to build the trace, multiplies the forward vector by a chosen range, and ignores the character by adding itself to the query params. Drawing a debug line with different colors for hit and miss makes it easy to spot mistakes. A key safety measure is checking whether the trace returned true or if FHitResult reports a blocking hit before calling GetActor or accessing the hit component. If you need per-bone detection for headshots, set bTraceComplex to true so the trace tests per-polygon collision. Keep in mind that toggling render custom depth requires the component to support it, so guard your casts and null checks. This walkthrough prepares you to integrate interaction traces into Tick or on-demand input handlers and to iterate with debug visualization until the behavior matches your design.

keyIdea.text: Use a line trace from the camera, ignore the player, check for hit, and toggle custom depth on the hit component for highlighting.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough Interaction Trace

Implementing UpdateInteractionTrace()

Starter snippet
#include "Kismet/KismetSystemLibrary.h" // For UKismetSystemLibrary::LineTraceSingleByChannel
#include "DrawDebugHelpers.h" // For DrawDebugLine

void AMyCharacter::PerformInteractionTrace()
{
    FVector StartLocation = GetPawnViewLocation(); // Or camera location
    FVector EndLocation = StartLocation + GetPawnViewRotation().Vector() * 200.0f; // 200 units forward

    FHitResult HitResult;
    FCollisionQueryParams QueryParams;
    QueryParams.AddIgnoredActor(this); // Ignore the character performing the trace
    QueryParams.bTraceComplex = true; // Trace against complex collision (per-poly) if available

    bool bHit = GetWorld()->LineTraceSingleByChannel(
        HitResult,
        StartLocation,
        EndLocation,
        ECC_Visibility, // Trace against the Visibility collision channel
        QueryParams
    );

    DrawDebugLine(GetWorld(), StartLocation, EndLocation, bHit ? FColor::Green : FColor::Red, false, 2.0f, 0, 1.0f);

    if (bHit)
    {
        AActor* HitActor = HitResult.GetActor();
        if (HitActor)
        {
            UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("Hit Actor: %s at %s"), *HitActor->GetName(), *HitResult.Location.ToString());
        }
    }
}
Explanation & safeguards
  • QueryParams.AddIgnoredActor prevents self-hits, which are a frequent error.
  • bTraceComplex=true asks for per-polygon collision useful for precise bone or limb hits; it is slower.
  • DrawDebugLine helps you see the trace during development and diagnose incorrect starts or ranges.
Highlighting flow
If the hit actor differs from the stored highlighted actor, un-highlight the old one, then set the new component to render custom depth and update the stored pointer.
Performance note
Avoid running this trace every frame for heavy effects; run on input or at reduced frequency when possible.
Key Takeaway

Use query params and debug drawing; check hit validity before using hit data and guard component casts.

screens.title: Line Trace vs Shape Trace
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between a line trace and a shape trace is a matter of intent and performance. A line trace is ideal when you need a precise one-dimensional check — for example, determining what a player is directly looking at or implementing hitscan weapons where the hit must be accurate along a single path. Shape traces, such as sphere, box, or capsule sweeps, are used when the interaction is volumetric: a melee swing that should hit any actor swept by the attack, or an explosion radius where you need to detect multiple objects within a volume. Shape traces return any collisions along the swept path and can be called in multi variants to retrieve all hits. Performance-wise, a single shape trace is generally cheaper and simpler than firing many line traces to cover the same volume. A common beginner mistake is approximating a volume by issuing multiple line traces in a fan pattern; this is both more error-prone and less efficient than a single sphere or box trace. Another difference is interpretability: shape traces may return multiple overlapping hits which you must sort or filter, whereas a single line trace typically returns one blocking hit. When designing interactions, choose the smallest shape that satisfies gameplay rules and prefer the engine’s built-in swept traces for area effects.

keyIdea.text: Use line tracing for precise single-target checks; use shape tracing for volume sweeps and multi-hit detection.

content.html:
Comparison Line vs Shape

Line Trace and Shape Trace

Line Trace (one-dimensional)
  • Precise look or hitscan behavior.
  • Typically returns a single blocking hit with location and normal.
  • Use for interactions where exact point matters, like clicking small objects or headshots.
Use case
Highlight object under crosshair or implement hitscan weapon logic.
Shape Trace (swept volume)
  • Detects objects within a swept shape like sphere or box.
  • Returns multiple hits in multi variants; useful for area effects.
  • Generally more efficient than many line traces that approximate the same volume.
Use case
Melee swings, explosion radii, or overlap queries for AI sensing.
Pro tip
When you need multiple hits, use the Multi variant of a shape trace instead of many line traces.
Common mistake
Issuing many line traces in a fan to approximate an arc instead of one swept trace.
Key Takeaway
Match the trace type to the interaction: precision or volume.

screens.title: FHitResult and What It Contains
screens.narratorSegment: FHitResult is the structured reply you get from a trace call. It packages information that enables gameplay logic: the actor and component that were hit, the hit location in world space, the surface normal at the hit point, and additional details like bone name for skeletal meshes. When you receive an FHitResult, treat it as data you must validate. The trace call returns a boolean or sets a blocking flag that signals whether a valid hit occurred. Only after confirming this should you call GetActor or access the hit component. Use the location and normal to spawn effects, compute impact responses, or align decals. If the target is a skeletal mesh and you need limb-level precision, query the bone name to determine headshots or limb hits. Note that some hits may not include a component pointer if the hit was against a simple collision primitive; be defensive in your casts and null checks. Common errors include dereferencing an invalid component pointer or assuming physical material is present; set QueryParams to return physical material only if you need it. Remember: FHitResult is rich and enables many effects, but it must be treated as conditional data that exists only when the trace actually hit something.

keyIdea.title: FHitResult
keyIdea.text: A container of hit details; always check for a valid blocking hit before reading fields like actor, component, location, normal, and bone name.

content.html:
Definition FHitResult anatomy

What FHitResult gives you

Fields to use
  • GetActor() — the actor that was hit, may be null if no blocking hit.
  • GetComponent() — the hit component; check before casting to specific types.
  • Location — world coordinate of the hit for spawning effects.
  • Normal — surface normal for orienting impacts or decals.
  • BoneName — for skeletal meshes when bTraceComplex is true and precision is required.
Practical considerations
Always verify the trace returned a blocking hit. If you need physical material, enable the option in query params. Guard component operations with casts and null checks to avoid crashes in gameplay code.
Example use
Use hit location and normal to spawn a particle effect aligned to the surface, and use the actor pointer to call an interaction interface if available.
Key Takeaway

Treat FHitResult as conditional data. Only use its fields after confirming a valid hit and guarding pointers.

screens.title: Collision Channels and FCollisionQueryParams
screens.narratorSegment: Collision channels let you control what your trace interacts with. Each primitive component has an object type and a set of responses to trace channels. For example, a wall may block visibility while a pickup item blocks a custom interaction channel. Define custom channels in Project Settings to separate gameplay concerns like projectiles, interaction, and camera occlusion. In C++, pass the chosen channel to the trace call to limit evaluations to relevant objects. FCollisionQueryParams further refine behavior by specifying which actors to ignore, whether to request physical material data, and whether to use complex tracing. AddIgnoredActor(this) is essential when tracing from the player so the trace does not immediately hit the character. bTraceComplex toggles per-polygon collision: set it true for precision such as limb or bone hits, and false for faster, simplified checks for general gameplay. Use collision profiling tools and debug drawing to confirm your responses. A typical pattern is to use a dedicated interaction channel for pickups that only relevant actors respond to, greatly reducing false positives and improving performance. The core idea: design collision responses and query params together so traces remain accurate and efficient in your gameplay systems.

keyIdea.title: Filtering
keyIdea.text: Use collision channels and FCollisionQueryParams to filter hits, ignore self, and choose complex collision only when necessary.

content.html:
Process Flow Collision & Query Params

Channels and query parameters

Collision channels

Choose a channel like Visibility or a custom ECC_GameTraceChannel1. Components declare object types and response per channel (Block, Overlap, Ignore). Use channels to make traces only evaluate intended actors.

Example
Set pickups to block your Interaction channel and use that channel for object pickup traces to avoid hitting static world geometry.
FCollisionQueryParams
  • AddIgnoredActor to prevent self-hits.
  • bTraceComplex toggles simplified vs per-polygon collision.
  • Optionally request physical material if surface-specific logic is required.
Misconception
Setting bTraceComplex true everywhere guarantees accuracy; instead, use it only where precise per-polygon detection is necessary due to performance costs.
Key Takeaway

Design channels and query params to reduce irrelevant hits and balance precision against performance.

screens.title: Performance Considerations and Debugging
screens.narratorSegment: Tracing can be inexpensive at small scales, but costs add up when you perform many traces, use complex collision repeatedly, or execute multi-traces across many actors per frame. A practical guideline is to limit traces to only when necessary: run interaction traces on input events or at a reduced tick rate rather than every frame. Prefer simple collision over complex when per-polygon detail is unnecessary. Use shape traces to replace many individual line traces when checking a volume, and use multi variants to collect all hits in one call. For debugging, the engine provides DrawDebugLine, DrawDebugSphere, and other helpers to visualize traces and swept shapes; color-code hits and misses to quickly identify incorrect start points, ranges, or ignored actors. Another useful practice is to isolate trace workload and profile it to see C P U cost. If you suspect traces are expensive, temporarily reduce their frequency and observe gameplay impact. Remember that correct collision setup — object types and channel responses — often reduces wasted checks, because the trace logic only evaluates meaningful actors. The checkpoint: balance trace frequency, complexity, and coverage so you get reliable interactions without introducing performance regressions.

narration.text: Tracing can be inexpensive at small scales, but costs add up when you perform many traces, use complex collision repeatedly, or execute multi-traces across many actors per frame. Definition Performance & Debugging

Keep traces efficient and debuggable

Performance tips

screens.title: Implementing the Highlight Interaction
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity guides you to implement an interaction highlight using a line trace from the player camera. First, add a member AActor* CurrentHighlightedActor to your character class and initialize it to null in BeginPlay. Next, create UpdateInteractionTrace and call it from Tick or when desired. Inside the function, compute StartLocation with GetPawnViewLocation and EndLocation by adding the forward vector times about 500 units. Configure FCollisionQueryParams, call AddIgnoredActor(this), and set bTraceComplex to false for highlighting. Call LineTraceSingleByChannel with ECC_Visibility and the query params. If bHit is true, get the actor from the hit result and compare it to CurrentHighlightedActor. If it differs, un-highlight the previous actor by disabling custom depth on its root component, then highlight the new one by enabling render custom depth and setting a distinct stencil value. Update CurrentHighlightedActor accordingly. If the trace doesn't hit anything and CurrentHighlightedActor is set, un-highlight it and clear the pointer. Test by placing static meshes in the level that block visibility and confirm the highlight toggles as you look around. This guided approach emphasizes safe checks, correct query params, and debug visualization to validate your implementation.

Implement the highlight trace

Step checklist

screens.title: Common Mistakes, Misconceptions, and Assessment
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners often make a short list of repeatable mistakes when working with traces. First, failing to ignore the tracing actor causes self-hits; always call AddIgnoredActor for the actor initiating the trace. Second, not checking the trace result before accessing FHitResult fields leads to null pointer errors; verify the boolean return or bBlockingHit first. Third, overusing bTraceComplex without need harms performance; reserve complex traces for precision cases like headshot detection. Fourth, approximating a volume by firing many line traces instead of one shape trace is inefficient and error-prone. For assessment, two practical questions clarify understanding. Question one asks which trace and query setting are ideal for limb-level detection. The correct answer is a single line trace using bTraceComplex=true so the trace tests per-polygon collision and can return bone names. Question two asks about a sweeping melee attack where multiple enemies can be hit; the correct answer is a sphere or box multi-trace, because a single swept shape collects all hits in one efficient call. When you practice, deliberately try the mistakes described and then fix them; inspecting debug lines and toggling bTraceComplex will make the impact of your changes obvious. That hands-on iteration builds intuition about correctness and cost.

Assessment Mistakes & Quiz

Common mistakes and assessment

Common mistakes
  • Not calling AddIgnoredActor(this) and hitting yourself.
  • Accessing FHitResult fields without checking for a valid hit.
  • Using bTraceComplex unnecessarily and paying the performance cost.
  • Replacing shape traces with many line traces instead of a single swept trace.
Assessment questions
Q1: For detecting limb-level hits in a shooter, which trace and query setting is most appropriate? Answer: Use LineTraceSingleByChannel and set bTraceComplex=true to check per-polygon collision and read bone names for precision.
Q2: For a sweeping melee attack that should hit multiple enemies, which trace is more performant than many line traces? Answer: Use SphereTraceMultiByChannel or BoxTraceMultiByChannel; a single swept shape collects multiple hits efficiently.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Keep three key concepts in mind as you design interactions. First, tracing is a query: it asks the physics system what a ray or shape intersects and returns an FHitResult; treat that data as conditional and check the hit flag. Second, choose the appropriate trace type: lines for precision, shapes for area sweeps; shape traces often replace many line traces and reduce runtime cost. Third, use collision channels and FCollisionQueryParams to filter hits, ignore the tracing actor, and decide whether complex per-polygon collision is necessary. Apply these ideas together—appropriate trace type, correct filtering, and careful hit handling—to build reliable, performant gameplay features like highlighting, shooting, and melee attacks. As a quick mental checklist: validate hits, avoid self-hits, prefer simple collision until you need precision, and visualize traces while debugging. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
Tracing, often called raycasting, is the backbone of many gameplay interactions. In this lesson you will learn what tracing means, how Unreal’s line and shape traces let C++ code ask the world what lies along a path, and why interpreting the result correctly is crucial. We will look at the line trace for precise, direct hits, and shape traces for area sweeps. You will also learn to read the FHitResult structure to find which actor or component was hit and where, how collision channels filter results, and how FCollisionQueryParams change behavior like ignoring the tracing actor and choosing complex versus simple collision. A concrete use case is highlighting an object when the player looks at it: a single line trace from the camera can locate the object and toggle a highlight. We’ll also point out common beginner mistakes, such as not ignoring the player or not checking for a valid hit, and discuss performance trade‑offs so your traces don’t become a runtime bottleneck. By the end you’ll be ready to implement and debug interaction traces in C++.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain what tracing is, implement line and shape traces in C++ and interpret the result to drive gameplay. You will learn to extract helpful information from the hit result such as which actor or component was hit and where, and why checking for a valid blocking hit prevents runtime errors. You will also configure collision channels and object types to precisely filter results, preventing traces from returning irrelevant actors. Finally, you will recognize common mistakes — like not ignoring the tracing actor — and apply performance best practices so traces do not slow your game. A concrete example to keep in mind is highlighting an object when the player looks at it: you will implement a line trace from the camera, ignore the player, check the result, and toggle a render setting to highlight the hit. Understanding these objectives helps you design interactions that are accurate, efficient, and maintainable in Unreal Engine C++.

These objectives map to concrete developer actions you will perform in C++. For describing tracing, practice by writing a short document or comment that explains a line trace and a sphere sweep and when to use each. For implementation, write functions that call the engine’s line and shape trace APIs, supply start and end positions or extents, and compile them into your player character. For interpreting hit results, add guards that check whether the hit was a blocking hit before accessing the actor or component. For collision and performance, create a simple experiment: add two actors with different object types and custom responses, then run traces that selectively hit only one type using channels. Finally, validate performance by running traces at different frequencies and observe C P U usage. Each objective is verifiable: you can unit test the logic that decides whether to highlight an actor, and manually confirm traces by enabling debug drawing. This active approach ensures you can not only explain tracing, but also implement, test, and optimize it in a real Unreal C++ project.

Tracing is the act of casting an invisible probe — a line or swept shape — through the game world to detect what it intersects. Think of a flashlight beam that reports the first object it hits. In Unreal Engine, traces are performed using C++ APIs that accept start and end points, or start/end with a shape size, and return an FHitResult containing who was hit and where. The practical value is broad: you use a line trace to detect what the player is looking at for interactions, and shape traces to test volumes such as a melee swing or explosion sweep. An important detail is that traces do not move actors; they only ask the physics and collision system which objects intersect the probe. This keeps traces cheap conceptually, but cost accumulates when you run many complex traces each frame. As a quick concrete example, if you want a player to pick up a key they see on a table, cast a line from the camera forward a short distance, check the hit, verify the actor implements your interaction interface, and then execute the pickup. A common misconception is to assume a trace always returns usable pointers; always check the hit flag before accessing actor, component, or hit location. The core takeaway is that tracing gives you precise information about line of sight and overlaps when set up with appropriate collision and query parameters.

Performing a line trace in C++ follows a clear sequence: pick a start point, compute an end point, configure your query parameters, call the trace A P I, visualize for debugging, and then interpret the FHitResult. Start by choosing the correct origin — typically the player camera or pawn view location — and compute the end point by adding the forward vector scaled by your trace distance. Next, set up an FCollisionQueryParams object to ignore the tracing actor and configure whether you want complex collision. Call LineTraceSingleByChannel on the world, supplying the collision channel such as visibility or a custom channel. The function returns a boolean indicating whether a blocking hit occurred and fills an FHitResult with fields like actor, component, location, and normal. Always test the returned boolean or bBlockingHit before using any pointers. Use debug helpers to draw a line in green for hits or red for misses; this visual feedback makes logic errors obvious. For multiple objects along the path use multi-trace variants. A frequent mistake is performing traces every frame unnecessarily; prefer running them on input or at a reduced frequency when possible. By following these steps you get a predictable, debuggable trace that converts into concrete gameplay responses, like picking up, highlighting, or shooting an object.

Now we walk through a practical C++ implementation that highlights an actor the player is looking at. The essential flow is: compute start and end, set up FHitResult and FCollisionQueryParams, call LineTraceSingleByChannel, and conditionally toggle the render custom depth on the hit actor’s root component. The example uses GetPawnViewLocation and the pawn view rotation to build the trace, multiplies the forward vector by a chosen range, and ignores the character by adding itself to the query params. Drawing a debug line with different colors for hit and miss makes it easy to spot mistakes. A key safety measure is checking whether the trace returned true or if FHitResult reports a blocking hit before calling GetActor or accessing the hit component. If you need per-bone detection for headshots, set bTraceComplex to true so the trace tests per-polygon collision. Keep in mind that toggling render custom depth requires the component to support it, so guard your casts and null checks. This walkthrough prepares you to integrate interaction traces into Tick or on-demand input handlers and to iterate with debug visualization until the behavior matches your design.

Choosing between a line trace and a shape trace is a matter of intent and performance. A line trace is ideal when you need a precise one-dimensional check — for example, determining what a player is directly looking at or implementing hitscan weapons where the hit must be accurate along a single path. Shape traces, such as sphere, box, or capsule sweeps, are used when the interaction is volumetric: a melee swing that should hit any actor swept by the attack, or an explosion radius where you need to detect multiple objects within a volume. Shape traces return any collisions along the swept path and can be called in multi variants to retrieve all hits. Performance-wise, a single shape trace is generally cheaper and simpler than firing many line traces to cover the same volume. A common beginner mistake is approximating a volume by issuing multiple line traces in a fan pattern; this is both more error-prone and less efficient than a single sphere or box trace. Another difference is interpretability: shape traces may return multiple overlapping hits which you must sort or filter, whereas a single line trace typically returns one blocking hit. When designing interactions, choose the smallest shape that satisfies gameplay rules and prefer the engine’s built-in swept traces for area effects.

FHitResult is the structured reply you get from a trace call. It packages information that enables gameplay logic: the actor and component that were hit, the hit location in world space, the surface normal at the hit point, and additional details like bone name for skeletal meshes. When you receive an FHitResult, treat it as data you must validate. The trace call returns a boolean or sets a blocking flag that signals whether a valid hit occurred. Only after confirming this should you call GetActor or access the hit component. Use the location and normal to spawn effects, compute impact responses, or align decals. If the target is a skeletal mesh and you need limb-level precision, query the bone name to determine headshots or limb hits. Note that some hits may not include a component pointer if the hit was against a simple collision primitive; be defensive in your casts and null checks. Common errors include dereferencing an invalid component pointer or assuming physical material is present; set QueryParams to return physical material only if you need it. Remember: FHitResult is rich and enables many effects, but it must be treated as conditional data that exists only when the trace actually hit something.

Collision channels let you control what your trace interacts with. Each primitive component has an object type and a set of responses to trace channels. For example, a wall may block visibility while a pickup item blocks a custom interaction channel. Define custom channels in Project Settings to separate gameplay concerns like projectiles, interaction, and camera occlusion. In C++, pass the chosen channel to the trace call to limit evaluations to relevant objects. FCollisionQueryParams further refine behavior by specifying which actors to ignore, whether to request physical material data, and whether to use complex tracing. AddIgnoredActor(this) is essential when tracing from the player so the trace does not immediately hit the character. bTraceComplex toggles per-polygon collision: set it true for precision such as limb or bone hits, and false for faster, simplified checks for general gameplay. Use collision profiling tools and debug drawing to confirm your responses. A typical pattern is to use a dedicated interaction channel for pickups that only relevant actors respond to, greatly reducing false positives and improving performance. The core idea: design collision responses and query params together so traces remain accurate and efficient in your gameplay systems.
